_meta.comment: Hand-authored tips that override the converter's auto-generated tips. Keyed by question id (d1_001, d1_002, ...). Each value is an array of 2-4 short tips. Re-running scripts/convert_test_bank.py merges these into data/domain1.json.

d1_001: Two-sided trap: A says 'IT will pre-audit' — but IT's continuous monitoring is a control activity, not auditing. D says 'auditor can never audit those systems' — but writing detection scripts isn't the same as designing the control framework.

CAATs scripts that flag exceptions are a tool, not a control framework. Sharing them doesn't compromise the auditor's ability to test the underlying transactions, business processes, and other controls.
When IS resources are shared with operations, ask: 'Does the auditor still have independent ways to test what isn't covered by the shared tool?' If yes, sharing is acceptable.
d1_002: A and D feel reasonable (more complex org → more data; familiar org → less data) but neither DRIVES data collection. They are factors that may inform the audit AFTER scope is set.
Purpose, objective, and scope are the audit's north star — every downstream decision (sample size, evidence type, time budget) flows from them.
When you see 'BEST factor for determining the EXTENT' of audit work, look for the option that defines the audit's boundary, not its difficulty or backstory.
d1_003: Trap is A: management is the auditee. Letting them set scope without an independent risk assessment compromises auditor independence — even if their suggestion turns out to be correct.
Management may SUGGEST areas of concern; the auditor must independently VALIDATE through risk assessment. Choice C does both — the assessment may well confirm new systems are highest risk.
Default response when management requests specific scope: thank them, then run a risk assessment. ISACA Standard 1202 makes this mandatory in planning.
d1_004: Audit risk is the umbrella concept: audit risk = inherent × control × detection. The phrase 'during IS auditing' signals the umbrella term, not one of its components.
If the question says 'during the audit / undetected', think audit risk. 'Before any controls' → inherent. 'Controls fail' → control. 'Audit procedures fail' → detection.
ISACA conflates audit risk with material misstatement risk — they're treating the broad 'will I miss something material?' question.
d1_005: Trap is A 'overlapping': sounds related but means TWO controls covering the same objective. That presupposes you have a primary control — in a SoD failure, the primary control is what's missing.
Compensating controls answer: 'We can't implement the ideal control — what else reduces this risk?' Small-team SoD failures almost always demand compensating controls.
Common compensating controls for SoD gaps: enhanced logging + supervisory review, periodic transaction sampling, independent reconciliation, mandatory vacations, job rotation.
d1_006: Trap is C 'fraud detection': it's a real benefit of CSA but a side-effect, not the primary purpose. Don't confuse outcomes with objectives.
CSA's core mechanism is shifting CONTROL OWNERSHIP from audit to business management — making line managers responsible for the controls they live with daily. That's why A wins.
ISACA explicitly distinguishes CSA from internal audit — CSA enhances audit work, it doesn't replace it (immediately rules out D as a 'shift to consultative').
d1_007: Trap is D 'customizable': sounds like the most flexible choice and tools sales pitch favorite. But the PRIMARY requirement is data accuracy without performance impact — customization is nice-to-have.
Auditing tools are 'guests' in production — if the tool degrades the system being audited, the audit itself becomes a business risk and may invalidate the data being captured.
CAATs evaluation order: 1) accuracy of capture → 2) performance impact → 3) compatibility → 4) flexibility/customization.
d1_008: Trap is C 'IT knowledge': feels right (“they know our systems!”). That's exactly the conflict — they have existing relationships and may have worked on the very systems they'd now audit.
Independence is the foundational requirement of any audit role — it overrides all other competencies. Technical knowledge can be acquired; lost independence cannot be restored mid-engagement.
When hiring auditors from operational areas, the screening question is always: 'Which systems and projects did you work on, and which fall under audit scope today?'
d1_009: Trap is A 'CAATs': closely related and effective, but CAATs is a TOOL category. Continuous auditing USES CAATs but adds the real-time + automated reporting layer — the difference matters for 'emerging' risk.
'Emerging' implies time-sensitive: quarterly assessments (B) are too infrequent, log sampling (C) has lag, ad-hoc CAATs (A) still requires you to RUN them on a schedule.
CISA pattern: high transaction volume + emerging risk → continuous auditing. Almost never sampling alone.
d1_010: Two-step distinction: are we testing whether a CONTROL operates correctly (compliance) or whether DATA is accurate (substantive)? 'Were accounts authorized?' is a question about a control — compliance.
Mnemonic: authorization, approval, segregation → compliance. Balances, totals, monetary values → substantive.
A and D are sampling METHODS, not test categories — they self-eliminate when the question asks 'which type of testing is this?'
d1_011: Trap is C 'control': auditors recommend controls but don't implement them. Detection risk is the only risk auditors directly shape — through their choice of procedures, sample size, and expertise.
Risk ownership map: inherent (business nature) → control (management) → detection (auditor) → business (executive/strategy).
Phrase giveaway: 'selection of audit procedures' or 'audit techniques' = detection risk every time.
d1_012: Trap is A 'review prior findings': feels rigorous and IS part of planning, but it's an INPUT to risk assessment, not a substitute. Prior findings tell you about old issues, not current risk landscape.
Risk assessment is the foundation that determines scope, resources, sampling, and procedures. Without it, you're auditing by intuition and exposing the function to coverage gaps.
ISACA Standard 1202 makes risk assessment in planning MANDATORY — not best practice, mandatory. That alone elevates D over the alternatives.
d1_013: Trap is D 'audit core service and dependencies': feels like the right place to dig in, but you can't audit a system you don't yet understand. SOA is a distributed black-box architecture — you must map first, test second.
Canonical sequence for any unfamiliar architecture: documentation review → mapping (services to processes) → controls assessment → transaction testing.
When the question asks for the INITIAL step on a complex system, the answer is almost always 'understand it' — never 'start testing it.'
d1_014: Trap is A 'delete all copies': auditors don't perform remediation. This violates independence (auditor performing operational tasks) and oversteps authority.
Auditor's job: identify → document → report risk to management → recommend prevention. Management decides on remediation, not the auditor.
Anytime an option has the auditor DOING something operational (deleting, blocking, installing, configuring, fixing), it is almost certainly wrong.
d1_015: Trap is B 'state audit objectives': engagement-specific objectives live in the engagement letter, not the charter. The charter is organizational, not project-specific.
The charter is an authority document — it answers 'who, what scope, what authority' for the audit FUNCTION as a whole. Not for individual audits.
Charter content priority: authority > scope > responsibility > reporting line. Procedures (C) and dynamic technology content (A) belong in audit methodology documents, not the charter.
d1_016: Two traps: B 'report to audit committee' jumps past diagnosis; D 'recommend the owner fix it' violates independence before scope is even understood.
Auditors investigate before they recommend: scope the issue (how many, which managers, what type of access) before escalating or proposing fixes.
CISA pattern: 'small number found' + 'something off' = perform additional analysis FIRST. Almost never 'report' or 'recommend fix' as the first step.
d1_017: Attribute sampling = compliance ('does the control exist / fire?'). Variable/stratified/difference = substantive ('how much, how often, by what amount').
Whenever the question is whether a control was applied (a yes/no question), the sampling method is attribute sampling. Always.
d1_018: Trap is D 'create additional sample data' — fabricating audit evidence is a major ethics violation. Auditors test what's there, not what they wish was there.
Trap is B 'report the finding' — premature; lack of available changes isn't itself a finding without further work. Adapt the test approach instead.
When the original test approach can't deliver assurance, change the approach (with audit management approval). Document why and what alternative was used.
d1_019: Trap is D 'consulting on good practices' — discussing principles doesn't impair independence; designing or building specific application controls does.
Trap is C 'project team member without operational responsibilities' — observation/attendance without operational role is allowed, just disclose.
The line is at HANDS-ON BUILD. Discuss principles → fine. Sit in meetings → fine. Implement, code, configure → independence impaired.
d1_020: Continuous audit's value isn't reduced effort — it's reduced LAG between event and audit response. Real-time monitoring → real-time correction.
Continuous audit shifts the audit cycle from periodic snapshots to ongoing surveillance, making issues actionable while still relevant to the business.
Continuous audit doesn't displace responsibility for control monitoring (rules out C); that always stays with management/security.
d1_021: Trap is A 'ensuring compliance with development methods' — that's QA's job. Doing QA's job doesn't impair QA. Correcting code DOES (now QA approves their own corrections).
QA's role is to inspect and report — not to fix. Same independence principle as audit.
Anytime someone validates AND corrects the same artifact, you have a separation-of-duties failure.
d1_022: The other three (skill sets, test steps, time allotted) are downstream of risk identification. You can't allocate skills/time/tests until you know WHERE risk lives.
Risk-based audit planning is the audit profession's central operating principle — every other planning decision is in service of it.
ISACA Standard 1202 mandates risk identification as the foundation of audit planning, not an optional good practice.
d1_023: Trap is A 'control design testing' — design testing answers 'is the control conceived correctly?', not 'is it operating effectively?'. Operational effectiveness needs substantive evidence.
Trap is C 'documentation inspection' — documents may say one thing, the actual operation another. Documentation review by itself is weak evidence.
Substantive testing examines the actual transactions and records produced — the most direct evidence of whether the control is doing its job.
d1_024: Same answer pattern as the planning-extent question (d1_002): data collection extent is set by audit purpose and scope, never by auditor familiarity, auditee evidence ability, or data availability.
If evidence is hard to find, the auditor finds an alternative method, not a smaller sample. Difficulty doesn't shrink scope.
Recurring CISA pattern: 'extent of audit work' ALWAYS ties back to audit scope/purpose, never to the convenience or familiarity of the people involved.
d1_025: Trap is B 'definite assurance' — definite/absolute is impossible in audit; CISA always uses 'reasonable'.
Trap is C/D 'all items' — covering all items isn't realistic or even desirable; the goal is coverage of MATERIAL items.
Audit always works with reasonable assurance + materiality. Anytime you see 'definite', 'absolute', or 'all items' in an option, eliminate it immediately.
d1_026: Trap is D 'request the IDs be removed' — auditor doesn't get to request operational changes. They report; management decides.
Trap is A 'inform audit committee' — premature; document and report through normal channels first.
Auditor lifecycle: identify → document → report risk → recommend → defer remediation to management. Steps 4+ skip ahead, step 1 (D) is operational interference.
d1_027: Compliance tests answer 'does the control work as intended?'. They don't measure efficiency (A) — that's a management metric, not an audit one.
Trap is C 'integrity of data controls' — that's substantive testing's territory. Compliance is about CONTROL operation, substantive is about DATA accuracy.
Mnemonic: Compliance → Conformance to design. Substantive → Substance/data accuracy.
d1_028: Trap is C 'integrated test facility' — ITF tests current processing as it happens, not historical retroactive analysis. The question asks about LAST YEAR's data.
Trap is D 'embedded audit module' — same issue: forward-looking, not retroactive.
Generalized audit software is the right tool for retroactive analysis of large historical datasets — it can recompute, stratify, and identify duplicates without modifying production.
d1_029: Trap is A 'create the procedures' — auditor writing the documentation is a textbook independence violation.
Trap is B 'end the audit' — lack of documentation is a finding, not a stop signal. The audit's purpose is to identify risk; absence of documentation IS risk to surface.
Auditors test what exists, including informal/undocumented practices. Then report the documentation gap as a finding so management can address it.
d1_030: The risk analysis loop: identify assets → identify threats + impacts → evaluate existing controls → assess residual risk → recommend additional controls. The question places you between threat identification and risk calculation.
Trap is C 'disclose to management' — premature; disclosure happens after the analysis is complete, not mid-flow.
Risk = (threat × impact) MODERATED by existing controls. You can't quantify residual risk until you know what existing controls already mitigate.
d1_031: Reliability hierarchy: independent third-party > auditor's own work > internal system-generated > management assertion > internet/general data.
Trap is B 'line management assurance' — single weakest evidence type because management has direct interest in the audit outcome.
The key word is 'independent' — the more disconnected the evidence source from the auditee's interest, the more reliable it is.
d1_032: Trap is B 'only preventive and detective relevant' — corrective controls matter too; they reduce damage even when prevention fails.
Trap is C 'corrective = compensating' — different concepts. Compensating substitutes for missing primary controls; corrective fixes problems after detection.
Controls operate at specific points in data flow (input, processing, output). Their collective effectiveness depends on which points are covered and which are gap.
d1_033: Trap is D 'testing user access rights' — system access is necessary but not sufficient. Real SoD failures often happen through workarounds, shared credentials, or informal task delegation that don't show up in access tables.
Trap is B 'org chart' — describes intended structure, not actual practice.
Observation reveals what people ACTUALLY do; interviews reveal what they THINK they do. Together they detect the gap between formal access and actual behavior.
d1_034: Trap is A 'obtain management approval of corrective action' — corrective action plan ownership belongs to management, but approval is not the auditor's role.
Trap is C 'assist management in implementation' — implementation assistance violates auditor independence.
The closing meeting is the auditor's last chance to validate facts before publishing the report. Errors caught here protect both auditor and auditee.
d1_035: Trap is B 'authorizations' — authorization happens at transaction time, not at reconciliation time.

Trap is A 'vouching' — vouching matches recorded transactions to source documents (record → source). Tracing matches source documents to records (source → record). Reconciliation needs the upward direction.
Mnemonic: Tracing follows the journey forward (source → destination). Vouching looks backward (record → original source).
d1_036: Trap is C 'dated screenshot from sysadmin' — admin can modify settings before screenshotting. Trap is A 'admin spreadsheet' — same risk + manual transcription error.
Evidence reliability key: who handled it? If the auditee handled it, it's tampered until proven otherwise.
The auditor should pull configuration data directly whenever possible. Auditor-acquired evidence ≥ third-party evidence > auditee-provided evidence.
d1_037: Trap is B 'authenticity' — checksums detect corruption/tampering but don't prove sender identity. Authenticity needs digital signatures or MACs.
Mnemonic: Checksum = Change detection. Doesn't authenticate, doesn't authorize, just integrity.
Layered EDI controls: integrity (checksum/hash) + authenticity (signature) + authorization (transaction limits) + nonrepudiation (full PKI). Each requires its own mechanism.
d1_038: Tests performed under audit standards beat third-party letters because letters are subject to interpretation and not always conducted under formal audit methodology.
Trap is D 'confirmation letter from outside source' — would be #1 if not for the explicit option of an external auditor's tests. Procedures > assertions.
Subtle CISA pattern: when the choice is between 'auditor-conducted procedure' and 'third-party signed letter', the procedure wins.
d1_039: Trap is A 'EDI trading partner agreements' — agreements are legal protection, not technical prevention. Contracts don't stop unauthorized packets.
Trap is D 'program change control' — applies to system changes, not to runtime transaction authentication.
Unauthorized transactions = authentication failure. When 'unauthorized' is the symptom, look for authentication-strengthening options first.
d1_040: Trap is B 'reports with sign-off' — a signature without follow-up evidence proves only that someone touched the report, not that they reviewed exceptions.
Effective review = look at exceptions + take action. The presence of action items is the operational evidence.
CISA pattern for control effectiveness: a control that 'fires' but has no follow-up is a control that doesn't work — verify the follow-up loop, not just the trigger.
d1_041: Functional acknowledgments are EDI-native — they confirm that the receiving system parsed and accepted the structure. That's the data mapping audit trail.
Trap is A 'key verification' — used in encryption and data entry validation, not in EDI data mapping.
Trap is B 'one-for-one checking' — verifies completeness of transmission, not the correctness of the mapping.
d1_042: Same as d1_017: authorization compliance → attribute sampling. The value of the PO doesn't matter, just whether it followed the matrix rule.
Trap is A or B 'variable/stratified mean per unit' — these examine value distribution. Authorization is binary (yes/no) → attribute.
The matrix gives a rule. Compliance with a rule = attribute sampling. Monetary impact = variable sampling. Almost never confused once you learn the cue.
d1_043: Trap is A 'review source code' — code review can identify potential errors but doesn't confirm what the system actually does in practice.
Trap is B 'recreate program logic' — duplicating logic is risky; the auditor's reimplementation may have its own bugs.

Black-box testing with known inputs and predetermined expected outputs is the cleanest way to verify any calculation — auditor doesn't need to understand HOW it computes, only WHETHER it computes correctly.
d1_044: Application control review's purpose is risk assessment — what can go wrong, and how bad would it be.
Trap is A or D 'efficiency / optimization' — those are operational metrics, not audit objectives.
Trap is C 'business processes served' — that's an audit prerequisite (understanding scope), not the focus of the controls evaluation.
d1_045: Trap is B/C 'do not include because resolved' — the audit report must reflect the period audited, not a snapshot at publication time.
Including the finding + the corrective action protects the auditee (shows responsiveness) AND ensures the issue is documented for future audits.
CISA pattern: the audit report is a permanent record of conditions found during fieldwork. Discoveries don't disappear because they were quickly fixed.
d1_046: Discovery sampling answers: 'has at least one occurrence of [event] happened?' — perfect for fraud screening (you only need to find one to expose a pattern).
Trap is D 'probability-proportional-to-size' — used when financial value matters; fraud screening is about occurrence, not value.
Trap is A 'stop-or-go' — used to limit sample size when expected exception rate is very low; not specifically fraud-tuned.
d1_047: The strategy phase identifies WHAT to focus on (areas, systems, processes). That requires knowing where threats meet vulnerabilities.
Trap is A 'controls in place' — that's an output of the audit, not an input to the strategy.
Risk-based strategy precedes audit; controls testing is what the audit does. Don't confuse the planning input with the audit deliverable.
d1_048: Trap is A 'sign release form' — confrontational and outside auditor authority.
Trap is D 'accept auditee position' — caves on professional judgment; auditee disagreement isn't grounds for retraction.
The auditor's job in disputes is to clarify the risk so the auditee fully understands what's at stake — then management can make an informed decision about acceptance vs. remediation.
d1_049: Trap is A 'schedule and monitor time' — operational, downstream of planning.
Trap is B 'train staff on technology' — staff capability is enabling, not the FIRST step.
Risk-based planning is the only thing that ensures audit resources go to high-value targets. Without it, you're optimizing the wrong thing.
d1_050: Trap is C 'include in report with comments' — premature; the auditor should first verify their own evidence before locking it into the report.
Trap is A 'retest the control' — retesting is downstream of evidence revalidation. If the evidence is sound, retesting may be unnecessary.
CISA disputes 101: when challenged, the auditor first verifies they have it right, then either confirms the finding or revises it. Never both publishes AND verifies in parallel.
d1_051: Trap is B 'avoid sampling risk' — sampling risk exists in BOTH statistical and judgmental sampling. Statistical lets you QUANTIFY it, not eliminate it.
Trap is C 'GAS unavailable' — statistical sampling is independent of the tool used; method choice is driven by the testing objective.
Statistical sampling's distinguishing feature is mathematical precision: it lets you calculate exactly how confident you are. Judgmental sampling can't.
d1_052: Trap is A 'revise per management feedback' — auditor doesn't revise findings just because the auditee pushes back. The IDS and firewall are different controls and don't address the monitoring gap.
Trap is B/C 'retract because IDS/firewall in place' — the question states monitoring is inadequate. Other controls existing doesn't substitute for the missing one.
The auditor considers management's input but doesn't auto-retract. Document the finding and capture management's response separately in the report.
d1_053: Trap is C 'compare checks to input forms' — checks reflect processed amounts, not what was input. Comparing processed → input loses visibility into the bank's transformations.

Trap is D 'reconcile checks with output reports' — both are bank-side outputs; reconciling outputs with outputs only confirms the bank is internally consistent, not that they processed YOUR data correctly.
End-to-end accuracy = compare INPUT (your data) to OUTPUT (bank reports). Same logic as substantive testing of any outsourced calculation.
d1_054: EDI's defining characteristic is automated electronic interaction with no human authentication step. That makes authorization the foundational control — without it, all downstream controls operate on potentially fraudulent data.
Trap is D 'deletion or manipulation' — also serious, but logging detects this. The authorization gap is more fundamental: it's prevention vs detection.
CISA pattern: 'GREATEST risk in EDI' is almost always 'unauthorized transactions'. Authentication and authorization are EDI's weakest link.
d1_055: Trap is D 'minimize audit resources' — resource efficiency is a benefit, not the primary goal of planning.
Trap is B/C 'collect evidence / specify tests' — these are outputs of the planning process, not its goal.
ISACA Standards mandate that planning must address audit objectives. Everything else (sampling, evidence, time) flows from that anchor.
d1_056: Trap is C 'all material weaknesses identified' — professional judgment can't guarantee this; reasonable assurance is the standard, not exhaustive identification.
Trap is B 'deficiencies will be corrected' — correction is management's responsibility, not the auditor's.
Professional judgment shapes the audit's evidence-gathering strategy: what's enough, what's relevant, what's reliable. The 'sufficient' bar is judgment-driven.
d1_057: Trap is A 'bar code readers' or B 'movement authorized' — these test CONTROLS (compliance), not the actual inventory state (substantive).
Trap is D 'check receipts/issues recorded' — same: testing the control over recording, not the records' accuracy itself.
Substantive = examining actual data/asset directly. Physical count IS the substantive test for any inventory.
d1_058: Trap is D 'encrypt orders' — encryption protects in transit, doesn't authenticate sender or validate order legitimacy.
Trap is A 'acknowledge receipt' — confirms transmission, not authenticity. Anyone can acknowledge anyone's order.
Authenticity = sender identity + content validity. Both must be verified. Contracts give the second-layer check (does this match what we agreed to?).
d1_059: Trap is A 'conclude inadequate controls' — premature; one inconsistent interview is a flag, not a conclusion.
Trap is D 'suspend the audit' — gathering MORE evidence is the appropriate response, not less.
When inquiry contradicts documentation, substantive testing is the tiebreaker. Look at actual transactions/records to see who's right.
d1_060: Recommending a specific product creates an appearance of vendor bias and compromises objectivity, even if no commercial relationship exists.
Trap is B 'organizational independence' — that's about reporting structure within the audit org, not external vendor neutrality.
Auditors recommend categories of solutions and required functionality; they don't endorse specific products.
d1_061: Trap is C 'identify control weakness' — too far ahead. Walk-throughs are scoping/discovery, not testing.
Trap is D 'develop risk assessment' — risk assessment uses business understanding as input, but the walk-through itself is the input.
Audit sequence: walk-through (understand) → risk assessment → scoping → testing → reporting. Each builds on the previous.
d1_062: The value of automated comparison is INDEPENDENCE from IS personnel — auditor doesn't have to ask 'what changed?'; the tool reveals it directly.
Trap is B 'detect change between copy and run' — incidentally true, but not the primary purpose of using the tool.
CISA pattern: when the question describes an audit tool, the answer is usually 'objective, independent verification' — that's the value tools add beyond manual inquiry.
d1_063: Trap is A 'overlooked issues' — the meeting isn't a comprehensive scope review; that should be done earlier.
Trap is C/D 'feedback on procedures / presentation structure' — these are quality assurance concerns, not the meeting's primary purpose.
Closing meetings exist to align on the findings BEFORE publication — getting auditee buy-in or surfacing factual disputes while there's still time to resolve.
d1_064: Trap is D 'review code migration procedures' — procedural review tells you what SHOULD have happened, not what DID happen.
Trap is A 'test data run' — verifies that the program produces correct output, not whether unauthorized changes were made.
Code comparison directly measures the ground truth: did the production code change between two snapshots? Procedures and outputs only indirectly reveal this.
d1_065: Trap is A 'IS management statements' — supplementary, not foundational. Statements without supporting evidence are weak.
Trap is B 'work papers of other auditors' — useful but should be validated independently before being relied on.
ISACA IS Audit and Assurance Reporting Standards require sufficient and appropriate evidence — that's the foundation of audit credibility.
d1_066: Trap is B/D 'efficiency' — efficiency is downstream of effectiveness; the structural problem is what threatens the QA function's purpose.
QA reporting to project management creates pressure to release defective products to meet schedule. Independence from PM is fundamental.
Same independence principle as audit: anyone whose work you're checking shouldn't be your boss.
d1_067: Trap is A 'audit committee' — the committee oversees the audit function, doesn't dictate report contents (would compromise auditor independence).
Trap is D 'CEO' — would convert audit into management's reporting tool, gutting independence.
The auditor decides what goes in the report. Senior leaders may push back, but the report is the auditor's professional product.
d1_068: Trap is C 'access rights' — access rights are about who can read the file; encryption is about whether unauthorized readers CAN read it once they have it. Different control layer.
Trap is A 'audit trail of versioning' — versioning is integrity, not confidentiality. Different security objective.
CIA mapping: encryption → confidentiality (and tamper-resistance). Access controls → confidentiality (preventive). Audit logs → accountability/integrity.
d1_069: Trap is A 'regulatory compliance' — secondary; following regulations doesn't replace the audit's epistemic purpose.
Trap is C 'complete coverage' — coverage is downstream; you collect evidence to support conclusions, not to fill checklists.
Audit conclusions must be defensible. Sufficient + appropriate evidence is the only thing that makes them so.
d1_070: Trap is B/C 'report to audit committee / management' — premature; need more evidence first to avoid false alarms.
Trap is D 'consult external legal counsel' — way premature and outside auditor authority.
Fraud indicators trigger ESCALATION OF AUDIT WORK, not immediate escalation up the chain. Verify before you alarm.
d1_071: Trap is A 'effective preventive control' — logging doesn't prevent anything; it records.
Trap is B 'valid detective control' — would be true IF logs were reviewed. Generation alone isn't a control.
CISA principle: logging without review is a non-control. Generation + review = detective control.
d1_072: Same as d1_015: the charter is organizational, not engagement-specific.
Trap is A/B 'engagement plans / objectives' — these belong in engagement letters, not the charter.
Trap is C 'training plan' — operational, owned by the audit director, not the charter.
d1_073: Trap is C 'compliance testing' — compliance tests examine whether controls were applied, not whether data is duplicated.
Trap is A 'attribute sampling' — sampling examines a SUBSET; duplicate detection needs full population coverage.
Duplicate detection over a full file is a CAATs job — automated comparison across all records, not sampling.
d1_074: Trap is A 'threat assessment' — threats are AGAINST something. You need the something first.
Trap is B/D 'data classification / criticality' — both require knowing WHAT's being classified.
Risk management starts with: what assets do I have? Then: what threats apply? Then: what's at stake?
d1_075: Same as d1_054: in EDI, authorization is the weak link.
Trap is D 'nonvalidated batch totals' — also a risk, but downstream of authorization. If unauthorized transactions are in the batch, valid totals are still a problem.
EDI security pyramid: authorization > integrity > nonrepudiation > confidentiality. Address the foundation first.
d1_076: CAATs is an umbrella term — the answer when the question asks for breadth across data sources.
Trap is A 'SQL' — only works on relational databases; can't access flat files, mainframe records, or proprietary formats.
When the question emphasizes 'diverse software environments', CAATs wins because of its tool-neutral, format-agnostic nature.
d1_077: The question's twist is 'exceptions for specific users' — that's a population characteristic. Stratified sampling lets you target user populations independently.
Trap is D 'systematic' — fixed-interval sampling can miss user-specific patterns if interval doesn't align with user distribution.
When a population has DIFFERENT subgroups with different risk profiles, stratify. When uniform risk, simple random or systematic.
d1_078: Trap is A 'decline' — too aggressive. Disclosure + alternative arrangements may suffice.
Trap is B 'inform after completing' — completely backwards. Disclosure is preventive, not retrospective.
Self-audit conflicts must surface BEFORE engagement starts so audit management can decide on safeguards (different auditor, peer review, scope limits).
d1_079: Trap is D 'preserve evidence of criminal activity' — preservation is part of the process, not its purpose. Forensics also covers civil disputes, not just crime.
Trap is A 'fraud investigations' — too narrow; forensics is broader than fraud (incident response, IP theft, data breach).
Forensic = methodical evidence handling. Purpose is systematic capture, analysis, and reporting (often for legal proceedings).
d1_080: Trap is A 'issue audit finding' — premature on a single observation. Could be isolated.
Trap is B 'seek explanation from management' — useful, but only after you've confirmed the pattern.
CISA pattern: a single observation is NEVER enough to issue a finding. Expand the sample to determine if it's systemic or isolated.
d1_081: Trap is A 'hire additional staff' — not always feasible in small orgs; the question explicitly mentions this constraint.
Trap is C 'log changes to development libraries' — detective only after the fact in development; doesn't prevent unauthorized production changes.
Compensating control for SoD failure: independent verification that production changes were properly approved BEFORE release. Same risk-reducing effect as full SoD.
d1_082: Trap is A 'identify systems and controls' — too early; you need business context to know which systems matter.
Trap is B 'list controls from program' — that's downstream of understanding what processes need protecting.
Risk-based audit starts where the business does: with strategy and operating model. Technology comes second.
d1_083: Trap is C 'note control deficiency' — premature; the diagram is being updated, not absent. No deficiency without a real gap.
Trap is A 'expand scope' — knee-jerk; first determine if these devices matter to the audit objectives.
Risk-based scoping decisions consider impact on objectives. New finding doesn't automatically mean new scope.
d1_084: System-generated > human-generated. Sysadmin spreadsheets and HR docs both have human handling and tampering risk.
Trap is D 'observations onsite' — useful but subjective and limited to what's observed live.
Reliability hierarchy applied: auditor pulls system-generated data directly = strongest objective evidence.
d1_085: Trap is A 'audit trails with date/time' — captures WHEN, not WHAT. Need transaction-level detail.
Trap is C 'user account administration' — administration metadata, not actual activity records.
When SoD fails, compensating control needs to capture activity at the granularity that would normally be checked. Transaction-level logs do this; metadata-only logs don't.
d1_086: Self-audit is a textbook independence violation. Even if technical work is fine, the appearance of conflict undermines audit credibility.
Trap is B/C/D — these are skill/competence concerns, all secondary to the independence concern.
Independence > competence. Skill gaps can be filled with training; lost independence cannot be restored mid-engagement.
d1_087: Trap is A 'communicate results' — too vague; communication isn't itself the OBJECTIVE.
Trap is D 'identify compensating controls' — that's audit work, not the discussion's purpose.
The findings discussion is the FACT-CHECK + REMEDIATION-START step. Two purposes: confirm accuracy, propose action.
d1_088: Trap is C 'facilitating training' — training delivery is education, not framework design. Doesn't compromise independence.
Trap is B 'advising on techniques' — advice on principles is acceptable; designing controls is not.
The line again: design and build → impaired. Advise, train, audit → fine.
d1_089: Trap is A 'stakeholders incorrectly identified' — operational, fixable.
Trap is B 'cost overruns' — efficiency concern, not effectiveness.
Without objectives, the audit has no compass — and the worst outcome is missing critical risk that goes unaudited.
d1_090: Trap is D 'heuristic scanning' — virus detection technique, not log analysis.
Trap is B 'embedded data collection' — captures data, doesn't analyze for anomalies.
Anomaly detection = pattern variance from baseline. Trend/variance tools are purpose-built for this.
d1_091: Trap is B 'don't report because out of scope' — material findings are reported regardless of scope.
Trap is D 'cease audit until resolved' — auditor can't halt operations or audits over a finding.
Trap is A 'inform IT manager + recommend solutions' — verbal only is weak; the finding must be formally reported. Recommending specific solutions also touches on independence.
d1_092: Continuous audit / automated monitoring requires aligning all key controls — that alignment naturally exposes redundancies.
Trap is D 'testing controls for effectiveness' — finds weak controls, not redundant ones.
Process redesign (automation) is the systematic way to surface duplicated controls; ad-hoc testing won't.
d1_093: Same pattern as d1_074: assets first, then threats/risk.
Trap is A 'review data classification' — already requires the assets to exist.
Trap is D 'cost-benefit analysis' — last step, after risk is calculated and controls are proposed.
d1_094: Trap is C 'inform senior management' — premature; need auditee agreement first to avoid disputes downstream.
Trap is B 'determine mitigation' — that's management's job, not auditor's first action.
Findings must be confirmed with auditee BEFORE escalation. Gets buy-in and surfaces factual disputes early.
d1_095: Trap is C 'replacement for audits' — CSA enhances, doesn't replace audit.
Trap is D 'management relinquishes control responsibility' — opposite of CSA's intent (it INCREASES management's control involvement).
CSA's main value: it's a high-frequency, low-cost way for the business to surface risk that audit then validates.
d1_096: Trap is A 'prioritize risk' — circular; you can't prioritize before identifying. The question literally asks what comes BEFORE ranking.
Audit universe = the inventory of things that COULD be audited. You can't rank what you haven't enumerated.
Pattern: any annual planning question starts with universe definition, then risk identification, then ranking.
d1_097: Same independence principle as d1_088 and d1_019: designing controls and then auditing them is a conflict.
Trap is D 'conducting vulnerability assessment' — that IS audit work, not a conflict.
Trap is A/C 'training / advising' — non-design activities are acceptable.
d1_098: Trap is A 'most valuable assets' — too narrow; assets serve processes, but processes are what you're auditing.
Trap is B 'audit resources' — too far ahead; you allocate resources after knowing what controls to test.
After process identification: identify control objectives → assess existing controls → test → report. Don't skip ahead to resources.
d1_099: Trap is B 'corporate standards' — internal, can't override law.
Trap is C/D 'good practices / org policies' — both yield to legal mandates.
Hierarchy of audit constraints: law > regulation > corporate standard > policy > good practice. Statutory always wins.
d1_100: Trap is A 'remove the auditor' — only required by some statutes; not always necessary if disclosure is made.
Trap is B 'cancel engagement' — extreme; disclosure usually suffices to address the conflict.
Trap is D 'restore independence' — independence cannot be restored mid-engagement; disclosure to the client is the proper recourse.
d1_101: Trap is D 'walk-through' — walk-through is best for understanding process flow but reperformance specifically tests whether the control performs as designed.
Trap is A/B 'interview / inquiry' — these gather information but don't test the control. Reperformance actually executes the control to validate it.
For automated controls especially, reperformance gives the strongest design evidence because the auditor independently produces results matching what the control should produce.
d1_102: Trap is A 'management concerns' — those are inputs, not the goal. Audit isn't a management consultancy.
Trap is D 'develop audit program' — the program is downstream of risk assessment, not its purpose.
Risk assessment in planning ensures audit attention goes to MATERIAL items — that's the materiality principle in action.
d1_103: Trap is A 'risk statement with business impact' — useful but follows from validated findings.
Trap is C/D 'recommendations / remediation' — these come AFTER findings are confirmed, not before.
Findings must be evidence-backed first. Without traceable evidence, audit conclusions can't withstand challenge from senior leadership.
d1_104: Same as d1_017, d1_042: yes/no compliance question = attribute sampling.
Trap is C 'stop-or-go' — used when expected exception rate is very low; not the primary tool for counting compliance failures.
The 'number of POs not approved' is a count of compliance failures = attribute sampling.
d1_105: CAATs make audit-collected data inherently more reliable because the auditor controls the collection.
Trap is A/C/D 'usefulness/relevance/adequacy' — these depend on the audit objective, not the data collection method.
CAATs primarily improves reliability through auditor-direct collection, removing the auditee-handling step that introduces tampering risk.
d1_106: Same theme as d1_022, d1_012: risk assessment is the foundation of audit planning.
Trap is B 'defining audit scope' — scope is determined BY risk assessment, not before it.
Trap is A/C 'audit program / information owners' — these come after risk assessment establishes the priorities.
d1_107: Audits ARE projects: scope, schedule, resources, deliverables, stakeholders. Project management skill is the umbrella.
Trap is D 'attention to detail' — necessary but operational, not strategic.
Project management skills cover audit constraint navigation; pure attention to detail doesn't address resource/schedule/scope tradeoffs.
d1_108: Trap is B 'replaces audit' — CSA never replaces audit. Just enhances.
Trap is C/D 'reduces workload / resources' — partial side effects, not the major benefit.
CSA is high-frequency, business-driven, so risks surface in real-time vs annual audit cycle. Speed of detection is the major benefit.
d1_109: Inherent risk = the natural risk before controls are applied. Number of users = scope of impact = inherent risk dimension.
Trap is D 'residual risk' — residual is what REMAINS after controls; the question asks why risk is HIGH from the start.
Number of users affected = exposure breadth = inherent risk dimension.
d1_110: Trap is A/B 'report to management / committee' — premature on a 'potential' finding.
CISA pattern: 'potential finding' = needs validation. Confirm before reporting.
Auditor credibility depends on never presenting unconfirmed findings as confirmed.
d1_111: Trap is A 'board of directors' — full board is too high-level; the audit committee is the board's delegate for audit oversight.
Trap is C 'executive management' — would compromise audit independence (the audit oversight body must be independent of management).
Audit committee is the board-level body specifically responsible for audit oversight, including the charter.
d1_112: Walk-through covers all the others (inquiry, observation, inspection, reperformance) for a process review.
Trap is D 'reperformance' — for end-to-end process understanding, walk-through is broader.
When the question is about evaluating a PROCESS (not a single control), walk-through is the canonical technique.
d1_113: Same as d1_057: physical comparison of actual data = substantive testing.
Trap is C 'analytical' — analytical compares ratios/trends; physical comparison is substantive.
Trap is B/D 'compliance / control testing' — those test controls. Comparing physical to records = substantive.
d1_114: Trap is A 'impact' — impact is the consequence of an exploit, not the gap itself.
Trap is D 'threat' — threats EXPLOIT vulnerabilities; absence of controls IS the vulnerability.
Risk vocabulary: threat (event), vulnerability (weakness), impact (consequence). Risk = function of all three.
d1_115: Trap is A 'do not report' — material non-compliance with documented procedures must be reported.
Trap is B/D 'recommend physical counts / new system' — premature; the issue is procedure non-compliance, not procedure inadequacy.
The auditor reports DEVIATIONS from documented procedures — improvement recommendations come AFTER understanding why the deviation happened.
d1_116: The condition is a SoD concern that needs to be reported, not analyzed or remediated by the auditor.
Trap is A 'recommend compensating controls' — premature; auditor reports first, management decides on remediation.
Same independence principle: developer + QA on related work is SoD violation. Report and let management address.
d1_117: Procedures embed SoD, dual control, and approval limits — that's where financial risk is addressed in wire transfer systems.
Trap is A 'privileged access' — only one piece of the picture; misses the transactional control framework.
Trap is C 'fraud monitoring' — detective control; the preventive controls in procedures are the primary defense against financial loss.
d1_118: When historical evidence is strong, you can accept lower confidence (more inherent risk acceptance) → smaller sample.
Trap is C/D 'higher confidence with larger sample' — that's for high-risk environments, not strong-control ones.
Sampling math intuition: confidence ↑ → sample ↑. Strong controls justify confidence ↓ → sample ↓.
d1_119: ISACA, IIA, IFA professional standards mandate supervision of audit staff regardless of staff experience.
Trap is A 'internal quality requirements' — they reflect professional standards, not the source of the requirement.
Supervision isn't about staff competence — it's a profession-wide requirement that protects audit quality.
d1_120: Observation directly verifies that two people are present during the operation.
Trap is A 'transaction logs' — logs may show two user IDs but don't confirm two PEOPLE were involved (one person could log in as both).
Trap is B 'reperformance' — testing the operation yourself doesn't validate the dual-control aspect.
d1_121: When controls are weak, you can't rely on them. Substantive testing examines actual data directly to compensate.
Trap is C 'compliance' — compliance tests verify control effectiveness; if controls are already known weak, compliance testing won't help.
Risk model: weak controls (control risk high) → can't rely on controls → substantive testing required to compensate.
d1_122: The initiation meeting establishes mutual understanding of what's in/out of scope.
Trap is D 'collect evidence' — way too early; that's fieldwork, not initiation.
Trap is B/C 'identify resources / select methodology' — those are audit team's internal decisions, not client meeting topics.
d1_123: Same as d1_015, d1_072: charter establishes the audit function's mandate — purpose, responsibility, authority, accountability.
Trap is A 'organizational structure' — that's an HR/governance document, not the charter.
The charter answers 'what authority does audit have to act?' — that's the foundational question.
d1_124: Trap is A 'technology architecture' — important but secondary; business context drives audit priorities.
Trap is D 'continuous monitoring' — that's ongoing operations, not audit understanding.
Audit always starts with business — what does this system DO for the business? That determines what to test and how deeply.
d1_125: Trap is D 'evaluate org structure' — shows formal structure, not actual practice.
Trap is B 'review IT job descriptions' — descriptions may be outdated or not reflect actual duties.
IT managers know who actually does what — direct discussion gives the real picture vs documents which describe intent.
d1_126: Approval before action = prevention. Manager approves before transaction processes.
Trap is A 'detective' — detective finds problems after the fact; approval prevents the problem from occurring.
Mnemonic: BEFORE → preventive. AFTER → detective. CORRECT after detection → corrective.
d1_127: Trap is A 'expand scope' — scope expansion needs authorization and may not be appropriate for minor issues.
Trap is C 'work with DBAs to correct' — auditor doesn't fix; reports the observation.
CISA pattern: any audit observation (regardless of scope) gets reported. Scope determines depth of investigation, not whether to mention.
d1_128: The system FIXES out-of-date PCs before allowing connection. Fixing = corrective.
Trap is C 'compensating' — would apply if it substituted for a missing control. This IS the primary control.
Trap is D 'detective' — detective only identifies; this acts on the identification. Detection + correction = corrective.
d1_129: Trap is D 'rely on management testing' — management self-testing doesn't replace independent audit.
Trap is A/B 'control design / operational testing' — not the question; the question is what to do with limited resources.
Risk-based prioritization is the right answer to resource constraints — concentrate where impact is greatest.
d1_130: Reperformance with same inputs and predetermined results is the gold standard for calculation correctness.
Trap is B/C/D 'walk-through / observation / documentation' — these don't independently verify the math.
CISA pattern: when 'effectiveness of calculation' is the test, reperformance wins.
d1_131: Trap is A 'process owners identify key controls' — process owners know controls but may not know cross-functional importance.
Senior management has the strategic view of what matters most to the business — they own the prioritization.
Risk-based planning starts with business process criticality — and senior management owns that picture.
d1_132: Trap is D 'perform an access review' — auditor doesn't do operational work; reports the deficiency.
Trap is B 'discuss with provider' — premature; report through the proper channel (IT management) first.
Material contract violations get reported in the audit report — that's the auditor's role.
d1_133: Same as d1_070: indicators ≠ conclusion. More work needed before reporting fraud.
Trap is A/B 'communicate / escalate' — premature; analyze first.
Trap is C 'report to authorities' — way too early; need professional evaluation first to avoid false accusations.
d1_134: Same as d1_074, d1_093: assets are the foundation of risk assessment. Identification + ranking comes first.
Trap is A/B/D 'threats / vulnerabilities / breach effects' — all are downstream of asset identification.
Pattern: every risk assessment chain starts with assets. Memorize: assets first, always.
d1_135: Badge entry stops unauthorized access at the door. Preventive control.
Trap is A 'security guard' — guards are deterrent (visible discouragement); badge system is the actual access prevention.
Trap is B/D 'IDS / fire suppression' — detective and corrective, respectively.
d1_136: Trap is C 'limited employee participation' — the OPPOSITE of CSA.
Trap is D 'policy-driven' — that's traditional audit; CSA is people-driven.
CSA = broadening control ownership across the business. Look for the option that emphasizes participation and stakeholder involvement.
d1_137: Trap is A 'censure deputy CEO' — outside auditor authority; punishment isn't the auditor's role.
Trap is C 'approve existing plan and circulate' — approving a 2-year-old untested plan is reckless.
The right action assigns ownership + sets a deadline. Definite responsibility + time limit = workable recovery from this situation.
d1_138: Trap is B/D 'cancel / postpone audit' — auditor doesn't halt the audit for findings; reports them.
Trap is C 'audit only DRP-covered systems' — ignores the gap, defeats the audit's purpose.
Continue audit + flag gap is the standard pattern when scope is incomplete.
d1_139: GAS filters and analyzes large datasets — exactly what threshold monitoring needs.
Trap is B 'integrated test facility' — tests current processing, not threshold monitoring.
Trap is C/D 'regression / snapshot' — not threshold-monitoring tools.
d1_140: CSA is structured, formal, documented assessment of controls — the most thorough ongoing maintenance mechanism.
Trap is A 'exception reporting' — reactive only, not proactive maintenance.
Trap is B/D 'manager oversight / peer reviews' — informal, less reliable than CSA's structured approach.
d1_141: CSA's defining feature: shifting control ownership from audit to management. Without that shift, CSA fails.
Trap is C 'stringent control policy' — that's traditional control approach, not CSA.
CSA is fundamentally about empowering business management — not about audit (D), not about staff managers (B).
d1_142: Table lookup PREVENTS invalid data from entering — input validation as prevention.
Trap is A 'transaction logs' — detective control.
Trap is B/D 'before-after image / tracing' — detective/audit techniques, not preventive controls.
d1_143: Embedded audit module = continuous evidence collection during processing. That's its purpose.
Trap is C 'identify fraudulent transactions' — a use case enabled by evidence collection, not the primary objective.
Trap is D 'increase efficiency' — side effect, not goal.
d1_144: The 'high availability' + 'multinational retail' setup signals high-volume environment where fraud detection speed matters most.
Trap is A 'preventive controls enforced' — continuous audit is detective, not preventive.
Trap is C 'errors corrected' — auditors don't correct; management does. Continuous audit only enables faster detection.
d1_145: Observation + log = direct evidence of the control firing AND being recorded.
Trap is B/C/D 'manual / interviews' — secondary; describe intent, not actual behavior.
Direct observation > indirect description for control effectiveness.
d1_146: Check digit is mathematically designed for transposition detection (swapping digits invalidates the check).
Trap is A/B 'range / validity' — these check value plausibility, not order accuracy.
Trap is C 'duplicate' — different error type entirely.
d1_147: Annual plan = resource allocation across the year's audits.
Trap is B 'reduce audit risk' — that's outcome, not purpose.
Trap is C/D 'training / cost minimization' — operational concerns, not the plan's main purpose.
d1_148: Same as d1_111: audit committee is the board-level audit governance body that approves the charter.
Trap is C 'audit steering committee' — steering committees execute, not approve charters.
Trap is A/B 'CFO / CEO' — executive management can't approve their own oversight body's authority document.
d1_149: Trap is A 'high-impact addressed' — close, but materiality (impact + probability) is the precise concept.
Trap is B/D 'efficient resource allocation / management concerns' — secondary outcomes, not the primary purpose.
CISA distinguishes 'high-impact' from 'material' — material includes both impact AND probability of occurrence.
d1_150: Trap is D 'discuss with auditee's manager' — confrontational and bypasses internal audit governance.
Trap is B 'retest the control' — premature; first consult internally to align on response.
Trap is C 'elevate the risk' — doesn't resolve the disagreement; just moves it up. Discuss with audit manager first.
d1_151: Data owner accountability spans the entire data life cycle — creation → use → archival → destruction.
Trap is A 'creating regular backups' — operational task, often delegated to custodians.
Trap is D 'risk assessment / implementing controls' — owners DEFINE requirements; custodians and security teams IMPLEMENT.
d1_152: Risk-based response again: prioritize highest-value areas with the available skilled resources.
Trap is C 'refuse to conduct audit' — overreaction; partial audit beats no audit if scope is communicated.
Trap is D 'extend timelines for training' — generally not feasible to retrain on the fly.
d1_153: CSA captures management's recent self-evaluation of the process — most current view of risk and current state.
Trap is A 'IT employee interviews' — too narrow; sample bias and limited scope.
Trap is C 'past audit reports' — historical, may not reflect current state.
d1_154: Risk-based planning calibrates testing depth to controls strength. Without knowing the controls, you can't plan testing.
Trap is B 'previous audit findings' — useful but historical.
Trap is D 'resource availability' — operational constraint, not strategic input.
d1_155: Information gathering precedes everything: business understanding, prior audits, current state.
Trap is A/B/D 'understand controls / compliance / substantive tests' — all downstream activities.
CISA always starts audits with information gathering and planning. Concrete activities (testing) come later.
d1_156: Trap is A 'change scope to exclude' — reduces audit value and may miss critical scope coverage.
Trap is C 'refuse audit' — overreaction; experts can fill the competency gap.
Trap is D 'proceed without skills' — violates professional ethics; competence is required by ISACA standards.
d1_157: Audit plans must be updated when scope changes are needed — with proper approval from audit management.
Trap is A 'inform cloud provider directly' — wrong path; client authorizes provider interaction, not auditor.
Trap is B 'ignore cloud backup' — assumes verbatim copy; auditors verify, don't assume.
d1_158: Logs reveal whether controls are firing as intended — if logs show gaps, substantive testing is warranted.
Trap is A 'control documentation' — paper exercise; doesn't show actual control operation.
Trap is C/D 'system specs / data flow diagrams' — design artifacts, not operational evidence.
d1_159: Data analytics enables population-level analysis impossible with manual sampling.
Trap is B 'eliminate testing/sampling' — analytics enhances, doesn't replace.
Trap is C/D 'reduce scope / add work' — analytics expands capability, not workload.
d1_160: Trap is B/C 'consult sysadmin / developer to fix' — auditor doesn't direct remediation.
Trap is A 'document in audit report' — too slow for an active zero-day exposure.
Active critical vulnerability needs management notification immediately to enable response — but management decides remediation, not the auditor.
d1_161: CSA can mistakenly substitute for audit — auditor must verify other controls exist and aren't being neglected.
Trap is A 'actively participate' — auditor would lose independence acting in the assessed function.
Trap is D 'recuse citing redundancy' — CSA doesn't replace audit, so audit role isn't redundant.
d1_162: Integrated audit's value is connecting IT findings to business consequences — speaks management's language.
Trap is A 'perform IT audits independently' — defeats the integration purpose.
Trap is B 'prioritize by complexity' — wrong driver; risk and business impact drive priority.
d1_163: QA programs provide the measurement framework for the audit function itself — a basis for evaluating effectiveness/efficiency.
Trap is A/C/D — all are activities OF a QA program, not its primary objective.
The objective IS providing the basis for measurement — that's what 'QA program' fundamentally means in process improvement.
d1_164: Without executive sponsorship, QA programs starve for resources and lose authority.
Trap is A/B/C 'systematic approach / clear objectives / continuous improvement' — implementation tactics, not the success factor.
CISA pattern: any program/initiative success ALWAYS depends on senior management commitment first.
